identification.summary: FIN13 is a financially motivated threat actor that Mandiant has tracked since 2017. Mandiant describes it conducting long-term intrusions against organizations in Mexico to gather information and carry out fraudulent money transfers, rather than smash-and-grab ransomware [S1]. Mandiant reports that the group relies heavily on custom passive backdoors, web shells and tunnelers rather than frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, with a median dwell time of about 2.5 years [S1]. Sygnia separately tracks an overlapping cluster as Elephant Beetle (TG2003), which it says steals millions of dollars from finance and commerce organizations, mainly in Latin America [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: tracked since 2017, with activity going back as early as 2016 [S1]. Sygnia: had tracked Elephant Beetle for about two years when it published in January 2022 [S2][S3].
identification.notes: Mandiant name: FIN13 [S1]. Sygnia name: Elephant Beetle, also tracked as TG2003 [S2][S3]. Secondary reporting on Sygnia's research states that Sygnia noted similarities or overlaps with Mandiant's FIN13 [S3]; MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as FIN13 (G1016) and the imported record lists Elephant Beetle and TG2003 as associated names [S7]. No Microsoft name for this actor was found in the sources gathered.

attribution.sponsor: None. Mandiant and Sygnia describe a financially motivated criminal actor; neither source makes a nation-state attribution [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant makes no nation-state or geographic attribution; it notes Spanish-language strings in the SHELLSWEEP web shell, the GASCAN fraud tool and targeted database artifacts [S1]. The FIN13 to Elephant Beetle linkage is stated by Sygnia as an overlap, not as an identity [S3].
attribution.basis: Mandiant incident-response data covering more than five years of intrusions [S1]; Sygnia incident-response engagements [S2][S3].

objectives: Financial theft: long, quiet reconnaissance of victim finance systems followed by fraudulent transactions, including point-of-sale and ATM-related fraud [S1]. Sygnia reports the group hides many small fraudulent transactions among legitimate activity to avoid detection [S2][S3].

regions: Mexico (Mandiant observed FIN13 operating exclusively against Mexico-based organizations over five years of data) [S1]
United States (secondary reporting says US-based firms were also affected) [S3]
targeting.notes: Mandiant says victims were large organizations, several with annual revenue in the millions to billions of USD, and that targeting a single country is rare: only 2.6% of financially motivated actors it tracks do so [S1]. Mandiant data is Mexico-only, while Sygnia's Elephant Beetle reporting extends to wider Latin America and some US firms; these cluster boundaries are not identical [S1][S3].

capabilities.summary: Initial access is primarily through exploitation of internet-facing servers. Mandiant saw indications of WebLogic and Apache Tomcat exploitation, though it could not confirm the specific vulnerabilities [S1]. Secondary reporting on Sygnia's research lists four exploited flaws: CVE-2017-1000486 (PrimeFaces), CVE-2015-7450 (WebSphere), CVE-2010-5326 and EDB-ID-24963 (both SAP NetWeaver). It also describes a focus on legacy Java applications on Linux, especially WebSphere and WebLogic, and obfuscated WAR archives [S4]. Mandiant documents a large custom toolset: BLUEAGAVE (a PowerShell/Perl passive backdoor), SIXPACK (ASPX tunneler), SWEARJAR (Java backdoor using DNS TXT), MAILSLOT (email-based C2), HOTLANE, BUSTEDPIPE, PORTHOLE, CLOSEWATCH, SPINOFF, DRAWSTRING, NIGHTJAR, LATCHKEY and a trojanized KeePass. Its fraud tool GASCAN sends ISO 8583 payment messages [S1]. The group also uses public tools such as Mimikatz, ProcDump, Invoke-WMIExec/SMBExec, NMAP and GOBOT2, and operates on both Windows and Linux [S1]. Sygnia reports more than 80 unique tools and scripts [S2][S3]. At publication, Mandiant had not seen FIN13 deploy ransomware [S1].

campaigns.name: Earliest observed FIN13 activity
campaigns.summary: Mandiant traces FIN13 activity back as early as 2016 and began tracking it in 2017.

campaigns.name: Long-term intrusions against Mexican financial, retail and hospitality firms
campaigns.summary: Mandiant observed long-dwell intrusions leading to theft of POS, ATM and treasury data. In one case GASCAN-driven ISO 8583 fraud produced more than 1,000 fraudulent transactions worth millions of pesos.

campaigns.name: Mandiant public disclosure of FIN13
campaigns.summary: Mandiant publishes its FIN13 profile with malware families and hashes.

campaigns.name: Sygnia disclosure of Elephant Beetle (TG2003)
campaigns.summary: Sygnia reports a financial-theft operation exploiting legacy Java applications against finance and commerce firms, mainly in Latin America, and notes an overlap with FIN13.

campaigns.name: AllaKore RAT campaign against large Mexican companies (tentative link)
campaigns.summary: BlackBerry reported an AllaKore RAT campaign using IMSS-themed lures against Mexican firms with revenue over $100M. SC Media says the activity is believed linked to FIN13, while other coverage calls the actor an unknown Latin America-based group.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated criminal operators with no nation-state attribution; Spanish-language artifacts appear in their tooling [S1]. Tracked as FIN13 (Mandiant) and Elephant Beetle/TG2003 (Sygnia) [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Exploits for internet-facing Java and web servers, including PrimeFaces, WebSphere and SAP NetWeaver flaws [S4]; custom passive backdoors, web shells and tunnelers; ISO 8583 fraud tool GASCAN; credential theft with Mimikatz and a trojanized KeePass [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised external-facing victim servers used as footholds; passive backdoors listening on high ports; C2 over unencrypted HTTP POST, email (MAILSLOT) and DNS TXT (SWEARJAR) [S1].
diamond.victim: Large financial, retail and hospitality organizations in Mexico [S1]; finance and commerce firms in Latin America and some US firms [S3]; POS, ATM, treasury and withdrawal-code databases [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven fraud concentrated in the Mexican and wider Latin American market [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Legacy, unpatched Java application servers (WebLogic, WebSphere, Tomcat) on Linux and Windows; payment-switch and POS systems using ISO 8583 [S1][S4].

gaps: Sygnia primary report and blog (blog.sygnia.co and the January 2022 PDF) could not be opened; Elephant Beetle details rely on press release listing and secondary coverage [S2][S3][S4].
Imported record lists country 'RU'; no cited source supports a Russian origin. Mandiant makes no geographic attribution and notes Spanish-language artifacts [S1]. Treat the origin as unknown.
Exact nature and strength of the FIN13 to Elephant Beetle overlap (shared tools, infrastructure or victims) is not documented in the sources gathered.
Some secondary coverage describes FIN13 as linked to ransomware, which conflicts with Mandiant's statement that it had not observed ransomware deployment [S1]; unverified.

The 2024 AllaKore RAT campaign link to FIN13 is tentative and contested in coverage; BlackBerry's original report was not opened [S5][S6][S8]. Later vendor reporting reportedly assigned this activity to a different named group; not verified here.
No public reporting found on FIN13 activity after 2022 attributed with confidence by Mandiant or Google Threat Intelligence.
NetWitness FIN13/Elephant Beetle paper and the MITRE ATT&CK G1016 page could not be fetched directly; MITRE data comes from the imported dataset [S7].
No Microsoft threat-actor name located for FIN13.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): Key terrain is internet-facing legacy Java application servers (WebLogic, WebSphere, Tomcat, SAP NetWeaver) and the internal finance systems behind them: payment switches, POS, ATM and treasury applications [S1][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Unpatched, years-old CVEs remain viable entry points, and multi-year dwell (median about 2.5 years) means compromise may predate current baselines [S1][S4]. STEP 3 (threat model): Exploit a public-facing server, drop a web shell or passive backdoor, tunnel inward, steal credentials, run reconnaissance on finance applications, then inject fraudulent transactions hidden among legitimate ones [S1][S2]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued quiet financial fraud against large Latin American organizations, including their US-linked subsidiaries [S1][S3]. MDCOA is long-term access to a financial institution or payment processor that serves DoD personnel or partner-nation forces in the region, enabling large-scale fraud or data theft. Candidate indicators: new JSP, ASPX or PHP files on Java or IIS servers; processes listening on high ephemeral ports (for example 65510-65512); unencrypted HTTP POST beacons to paths like /cpl/api.php; DNS TXT C2; anomalous ISO 8583 traffic or bursts of small transactions [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: FIN13 targets commercial and financial entities rather than DoD networks, so relevance is mainly to mission partners, contractors and financial services supporting operations in the USSOUTHCOM and USNORTHCOM areas; track legacy Java-server exposure on DODIN-adjacent systems [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: this is criminal activity, so response falls primarily to law enforcement and partner-nation authorities, not military cyber forces; DoD's role is defensive hardening and information sharing. (3) Mission assurance: multi-year dwell argues for compromise-assessment hunts on legacy application servers, not just patching [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, the DIB CS program and partner-nation CERTs in Mexico and Latin America.
